reason: A five-word run and the only candidate the machine offered for the verse that announces the sign. “for the space of” does occur in exactly one KJV verse — the King James Bible otherwise says 'by the space of' and 'about the space of' — so the rarity is real and it is worthless. “the space of” occurs in exactly sixteen KJV verses and is the KJV's standing way of measuring any interval; Acts 19:8 measures three months of synagogue preaching at Ephesus, and the preposition in front of it is an accident of English. 3 Nephi 8 uses the formula four times over — three days at 8:3 and 8:23, three hours twice at 8:19 — and the one occurrence that carries a real borrowing is 8:19's, where the run is longer and lands on a KJV singleton (Acts 5:7, 'about the space of three hours'). This entry covers every 'for the space of' candidate in the chapter.

sharedText: in the fourth day of the
reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter (rarity 3.04, a seven-word longest run) and it is a date. Zechariah 7:1 dates a prophecy to the fourth year of Darius and the fourth day of the ninth month; 3 Nephi 8:5 dates a storm to the thirty-fourth year, the first month, the fourth day. Both are the KJV's ordinal dating formula and the coincidence is the numeral 'fourth', which is the only rare word in the match. The same applies to 2 Chronicles 3:2, ranked below it for the same reason. The Book of Mormon dates its own chapters this way throughout (3 Nephi 1:1, 2:5, 4:5, 7:23 and the rest), so the formula cannot be a borrowing from whichever KJV verse happens to share a numeral with it — the standing exclusion at Helaman 1:1 makes this point for regnal dating and it holds here for calendar dating.

sharedText: into the depths of the sea
reason: A six-word run and the sole candidate for the verse, and the senses are opposed at the only point that matters. “depths of the sea” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Micah 7:19, Psalm 68:22 and Matthew 18:6 — and Micah's is the one that is quoted: 'thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea', the closing image of a book about forgiveness, where what sinks is guilt and the sinking is mercy. 3 Nephi 8:9 sinks a city with its inhabitants in it and drowns them. Matthew 18:6 is closer in sense (a millstone and a drowning) and shares less wording, and Revelation 18:21, where an angel casts a millstone into the sea as a sign of 'that great city Babylon' thrown down, is closer still in situation and shares nothing at all. “were drowned” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 18:6 and Hebrews 11:29, and the second is the Book of Mormon's usual Red Sea source (see 1 Nephi 4:2) — the Egyptians drowned, which fits an Exodus-plague chapter, but 'the inhabitants thereof were drowned' shares no further word with it. Nothing here rises above the vocabulary any English writer would use for a city going under.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue. 'The whole face of the earth' is one of the Book of Mormon's own most-worn phrases and 3 Nephi 8 uses it or a variant at 8:12, 8:17, 8:18, 8:20 and 8:22; the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 covers this class. Genesis 2:6 waters the whole face of the ground with a mist rising from the earth, which is a creation, not a destruction, and the only reason it ranked at all is that the Book of Mormon happens to have 'the whole face of the land was changed' in the same clause as a list of storms. Ezekiel 34:6's 'upon all the face of the earth', ranked at 8:18 for the same reason, is covered by this entry.

sharedText: the earth and the inhabitants thereof
reason: A six-word run, and it needs an entry rather than silence because Isaiah 40 is genuinely in play one verse earlier: 3 Nephi 8:13 is catalogued to Isaiah 40:4 by way of 1 Nephi 17:46, and a reader who sees the machine propose Isaiah 40:22 here will reasonably wonder whether the chapter is working through Isaiah 40 in order. It is not. Isaiah 40:22 is the grasshopper verse — God enthroned above the circle of the earth, stretching the heavens out as a curtain — and its 'the inhabitants thereof' is a genitive of the whole earth's population, while 3 Nephi 8:14's is a genitive of individual cities, repeated from 8:9 where the inhabitants of Moroni drown. 'Inhabitants thereof' occurs in the KJV too often to identify anything. The Isaiah 40 material this chapter actually uses is at 8:13, and it comes through the Book of Mormon, not straight off the page.

sharedText: (the unprecedented earthquake and the fallen cities)
reason: This is the register's most tempting entry for the chapter and the machine never proposed it. Revelation 16:18-19 is, on paper, 3 Nephi 8 in miniature: 'there were voices, and thunders, and lightnings; and there was a great earthquake, such as was not since men were upon the earth, so mighty an earthquake, and so great. And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell.' The chapter has the thunders and lightnings (8:12, 8:17), the unprecedented convulsion (8:5, 8:7), the fallen cities (8:14) and a great city named twice in the lament (8:24, 8:25), and “since men were upon the earth” and “cities of the nations” are each KJV singletons. Not one of those singletons is reproduced. The Book of Mormon's superlative is 'such an one as never had been known in all the land', which is the shape of Exodus 9:24 and 11:6 and not of Revelation's 'such as was not since men were upon the earth'; its list is 'thunderings' with the definite article, which is Exodus 20:18's form and not Revelation's articleless 'thunders'; and its cities are sunk, burned and shaken rather than divided and fallen. The seventh bowl and the Nephite destruction are two descriptions of one kind of event, and a shared kind is not dependence. Filed at length so that a reader who reaches Revelation 16 on their own is told the catalogue got there and could not make the wording work.

A four-word run, and worth an entry because the surrounding verses of Nahum are a better fit than the ranked one and still not good enough. Nahum 1:3 says the LORD 'hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm' — and “in the whirlwind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, this one, while 3 Nephi 8:16 has people 'carried away in the whirlwind'. Nahum 1:5-6 then has the mountains quaking, the earth burned at his presence and 'the rocks are thrown down by him', which is a KJV singleton and is three of this chapter's four disasters. But the Book of Mormon's rocks are 'rent in twain' and 'broken up', which are Matthew 27:51's and Helaman 14:22's words and not Nahum's, and its whirlwind carries people off rather than serving as God's road. The theophany of Nahum 1 and the destruction of 3 Nephi 8 share their furniture and none of their sentences.

The mourners' cry is a city-lament in two parts, spoken 'in one place' and then 'in another place', naming a burned city (8:24) and a buried one (8:25) and each time with the demonstrative: 'that great city Zarahemla', 'that great city Moronihah'. The King James Bible's stock city-lament has exactly that form — 'Alas, alas that great city' at Revelation 18:10, 18:16 and 18:19, twice with the city's name appended ('that great city Babylon', 18:10 and 18:21) — and Revelation 18 laments a city burned (18:9, 'the smoke of her burning'), mourned by weeping and wailing (18:19), and thrown down into the sea like a millstone (18:21), which is 3 Nephi 8:8, 8:23 and 8:9 in order. It is nevertheless declined. “that great city” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses, three of them Jonah's Nineveh, and the demonstrative-plus-name construction is ordinary English that the Book of Mormon uses of its own cities elsewhere. More decisively, the one phrase the lament repeats verbatim in both halves is not Revelation's: it is 'before this great and terrible day', which the mediation test refers to Joel 2:31, and the rest of the cry is Helaman 13:33's scripted lament word for word. The lament's form is Revelation's; its words are Joel's and Samuel's, and the catalogue records where the words are. See the links at 3 Nephi 8:24 and 8:25.

sharedText: (the mountain that falls on the mourners)
reason: Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it, which is the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' case again. On the way to the cross Jesus turns to the women of Jerusalem — 'weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children' — and tells them that they will say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us (Luke 23:28-30). 3 Nephi 8:25 is a crowd weeping in the crucifixion darkness for their mothers, their daughters and their children, who have been 'buried up in that great city Moronihah' — the city over which, at 8:10, the earth was carried up until 'there became a great mountain'. A mountain has literally fallen on and covered them, in the chapter that narrates the crucifixion, three verses after a lament shaped like Luke's. And there is not one shared word. mediation-check.py cannot even run the test properly: Luke 23:30 quotes Hosea 10:8 and reverses its verbs — Hosea has 'to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us', Luke has them the other way round — so the wording is decidable in principle, and 3 Nephi reproduces neither form, having no mountains address and no imperative at all. Recorded so that a reader who sees the type is told the catalogue saw it, could not settle which of Hosea and Luke it would point to if it were real, and declined it as dependence.

A four-word run of connective English. Exodus 18:8 is Moses recounting to Jethro 'all the travail that had come upon them by the way'; 3 Nephi 8:23 is the destruction 'which had come upon them'. The phrase is the ordinary KJV way of saying that something happened to somebody and it carries no argument in either direction. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; listed only because it was the verse's second-ranked candidate and the verse itself carries a real link (Amos 8:3).

A five-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse. Numbers 25:1 is Israel at Shittim beginning to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab; 3 Nephi 8:3 is a people beginning to watch for a sign. 'The people began to' is a narrative hinge, not a phrase, and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.
